modules.title: Hyper-V Deep Dive
modules.summary: The Windows-native hypervisor: vSwitches, VHDX, checkpoints vs backups, clustering, and performance tuning. Interview-critical for Windows shops. You need this for -> M19/M34 and the homelab.
objectives: Design virtual switches (external/internal/private) and explain NIC teaming.
Choose VHDX types (fixed/dynamic/differencing) and virtual hardware generations.
Use checkpoints correctly and explain why they are not backups.
Build a Hyper-V failover cluster with Cluster Shared Volumes.
Troubleshoot performance: dynamic memory, vCPU oversubscription, storage QoS.

notes.title: Architecture and virtual networking
notes.body:
Hyper-V architecture: Type-1 hypervisor - the hypervisor sits on hardware, and the 'host' Windows (management OS / parent partition) is itself virtualized. Child partitions (VMs) get virtual devices via the VMBus (fast, enlightened) or emulated devices (slow, legacy).

Virtual switches: External (bound to a physical NIC - VMs reach the LAN/internet), Internal (host<->VMs only), Private (VMs<->VMs only). Production pattern: external vSwitch on teamed NICs (SET - Switch Embedded Teaming), separate vSwitch or VLANs for management/Live Migration/storage traffic. VLAN tagging on vSwitch ports segments VM traffic without extra hardware.

Generation matters: Gen 2 VMs (UEFI, Secure Boot, faster boot, SCSI boot) for all modern OSes; Gen 1 only for legacy. Secure Boot + vTPM + Shielded VMs for sensitive workloads. Integration Services (guest enlightenments) must be current - mismatched versions cause weird performance bugs.

notes.title: Storage: VHDX done right
notes.body:
VHDX (not legacy VHD): 64TB max, power-failure resilience, 4KB alignment. Types: Fixed (preallocated - best performance, predictable), Dynamic (grows on demand - space efficient, slight overhead), Differencing (child tracks changes vs parent - great for labs/VDI, never for production data).

Placement: CSVs (Cluster Shared Volumes) for clustered hosts - all nodes read/write simultaneously. Pass-through disks are legacy; use VHDX on CSV. Storage QoS policies cap noisy VMs. Deduplication on VHDX libraries saves enormous space for golden images.

Checkpoints (snapshots): point-in-time differencing chains for 'let me try this risky change'. They are NOT backups: they live on the same storage, chains degrade performance, and production checkpoints left for months are a classic outage cause. Rule: checkpoints for changes measured in hours, backups for everything else; merge/delete promptly.

notes.title: Clustering, HA, and performance
notes.body:
Failover clustering: 2+ Hyper-V hosts + shared storage (CSV) or Storage Spaces Direct. Quorum (witness: disk/file/cloud) decides who survives a split - even node counts need one. Quick Migration (pause, move, resume - brief downtime) vs Live Migration (zero downtime - needs fast network, ideally RDMA/SMB Direct for storage).

Dynamic Memory: ballooning gives VMs memory on demand within min/max - great for consolidation, dangerous for SQL/Exchange (use static for memory-hungry apps). vCPU oversubscription: 4:1 to 8:1 typical for light VMs; monitor hypervisor CPU wait time - high wait = oversubscribed.

Replica (Hyper-V Replica): async VM replication to a second site every 30s/5m/15m - the poor man's DR (M31 deep-dives DR). NUMA: keep VM memory within one NUMA node when possible (vNUMA); spanning nodes costs latency. Measure with Performance Monitor: Hyper-V Hypervisor Logical Processor, Virtual Storage Device counters.

cards.back: Type-1: hypervisor on hardware; management OS is itself virtualized.

cards.front: External vs Internal vs Private vSwitch
cards.back: External: LAN/internet. Internal: host-VMs. Private: VMs only.
UEFI, Secure Boot, faster boot, SCSI boot - default for modern OSes.

cards.front: Fixed vs Dynamic vs Differencing VHDX
cards.back: Fixed: performance. Dynamic: space efficiency. Differencing: labs/VDI, not production.
Same storage, chain performance decay, left for months = outages.
Breaks ties in split-brain; even-node clusters need one.
Quick: brief downtime. Live: zero downtime.
Great for consolidation; use static for SQL/Exchange-like workloads.

choices: External vSwitch on teamed NICs + separate management network/VLAN
quiz.explain: Segmented virtual networking with teaming for resilience.

quiz.explain: Fixed avoids growth overhead on latency-sensitive workloads.

quiz.q: Checkpoint chain 6 months old on a production VM. Risk?
choices: Performance decay + storage risk; merge/delete promptly
quiz.explain: Checkpoints are short-term change tools, not archives.

quiz.q: Two-node cluster, network split between nodes. Who stays up?
quiz.explain: Quorum decides; without a witness both may fence.

quiz.q: VMs show high hypervisor CPU wait time. Meaning?
choices: vCPU oversubscription - too many vCPUs for physical cores
quiz.explain: Wait time = VMs queuing for physical CPU.

quiz.q: Zero-downtime host maintenance needs:
quiz.explain: Live Migration moves running VMs with no downtime.

quiz.q: Hyper-V Replica gives you:
choices: Async DR copy to a second site (30s/5m/15m)
quiz.explain: Async replication = affordable DR, some data-loss window.

quiz.q: VM memory spanning NUMA nodes causes:
choices: Latency - keep VMs within a node (vNUMA)
quiz.explain: Cross-node memory access is slower.

objectives: Compare Hyper-V, ESXi, and VirtualBox and choose per scenario.

notes.title: The three platforms
notes.body:
ESXi/vSphere: the enterprise standard for two decades - bare-metal ESXi hosts managed by vCenter, with vMotion (live migration), DRS (automatic load balancing), HA (VM restart on host failure), and vSAN (hyperconverged storage). Richest ecosystem, historically priciest; Broadcom's acquisition changed licensing (subscription, per-core) - many shops are re-evaluating, which is why Hyper-V and Proxmox knowledge now pays.

Hyper-V: Windows-native, licensed with Windows Server, excellent for Windows shops (M18). VirtualBox: free, cross-platform type-2 hypervisor - perfect for portable labs on a laptop, not for production. Proxmox VE: the open-source rising star (KVM+LXC, clustering, Ceph) - worth knowing exists.

Interview framing: 'I've run production on Hyper-V, labbed vSphere concepts, and keep a VirtualBox lab for portability.' Breadth + honesty beats claiming vCenter expertise you don't have.

notes.title: vSphere concepts that transfer
notes.body:
Even if you never touch vCenter, its concepts are the industry vocabulary: Cluster (group of hosts), Resource Pool (CPU/RAM reservations/limits), Datastore (shared storage), vMotion (live migrate), Storage vMotion (live migrate storage), DRS (auto-balance VMs across hosts), HA (restart VMs when a host dies - not zero-downtime; that's Fault Tolerance, 1:1 shadow VM).

Templates + cloning: golden templates -> rapid VM deployment; customization specs handle SID/hostname (the vSphere answer to sysprep). Snapshots: same rules as Hyper-V checkpoints (short-term only). vSwitch/dvSwitch: standard vs distributed virtual switching - distributed = centrally managed across hosts.

These map 1:1 to Hyper-V concepts (cluster, CSV, Live Migration, templates) - learn the mapping and you can talk to any virtualization admin.

notes.title: VirtualBox lab craft
notes.body:
VirtualBox: free type-2 hypervisor for Windows/Mac/Linux. Networking modes: NAT (VMs out, host-only inbound), Bridged (VM on the LAN like a physical box), Host-only (VM<->host), Internal (VMs only). Snapshots with branching - great for lab experiments.

Lab craft: linked clones (differencing-like, fast lab builds), host-only networks for isolated AD labs, port forwarding for NAT access, shared folders for file exchange, and exporting appliances (OVA) to share lab builds. Performance: enable VT-x/AMD-V, use fixed VHD for heavy VMs, don't oversubscribe a laptop.

V2V migration: convert VHDX<->VMDK with StarWind V2V or qemu-img; VMware vCenter Converter (retired - now use alternatives); always sysprep/generalize Windows when cloning across platforms to avoid SID/duplication issues.

cards.back: vMotion: live migrate. DRS: auto-balance. HA: restart VMs on host failure.
HA: restart (brief outage). FT: shadow VM (zero downtime, 1:1 cost).
NAT: outbound only. Bridged: VM is a LAN citizen.
vSphere moved to subscription per-core; shops re-evaluating alternatives.
vMotion.
Datastore (shared clustered storage).
Short-term change safety only - never a backup, merge promptly.
StarWind V2V, qemu-img; sysprep Windows when cloning.

quiz.explain: vMotion = live migration.

quiz.explain: HA restarts (brief outage); FT would have zero downtime.

quiz.explain: Isolated VM networks without LAN leakage.

modules.title: Containers & Docker for Infra Admins
modules.summary: What containers change for infrastructure: images, Docker workflow, Compose, and when containers beat VMs. You need this for -> M21/M22 and modern deployment conversations.
objectives: Explain containers vs VMs (kernel sharing, density, immutability).
Run and manage containers: images, volumes, networks, Compose.

Decide containers vs VMs per workload.
Describe Kubernetes' role at a conversational level.

notes.title: Containers vs VMs: the mental model
notes.body:
VM: full guest OS per workload (GBs, minutes to boot). Container: shares the host kernel, packages app + dependencies (MBs, seconds to start). Density: dozens of containers where a few VMs fit. Immutability: containers are rebuilt from images, not patched in place - 'cattle, not pets' taken literally.

Images are layered filesystems (each Dockerfile instruction = a layer, cached). Containers are ephemeral instances of images; state lives in volumes (persisted) or dies with the container. This changes backup thinking: you back up VOLUMES and image definitions, not containers.

For infra admins, containers shine for: lab services (spin up a test web server in seconds), CI/CD agents, and portable tooling. They don't replace VMs for: Windows AD, stateful monoliths needing full OS control, or workloads needing kernel isolation.

notes.title: Docker workflow that matters
notes.body:
Core loop: docker pull (image) -> docker run (container) -> docker ps/logs/exec (operate) -> docker stop/rm. Volumes: -v data:/data persists beyond the container. Networks: bridge (default), host, custom - containers get DNS by name on user-defined networks.

Dockerfile craft: FROM a minimal official base, one concern per layer, order instructions by change frequency (deps first for cache), COPY not ADD, run as non-root (USER), .dockerignore to keep secrets out. Multi-stage builds: compile in one stage, ship only the binary - tiny, safer images.

Compose: docker-compose.yml defines multi-container apps (web + db + cache) with one command. The homelab superpower: your entire monitoring stack (M33) or test environment as one Compose file - versioned, reproducible, shareable.

notes.title: Security and the Kubernetes conversation
notes.body:
Container security for infra: never run as root inside, scan images (known CVEs in base layers), pin versions (never :latest in production), keep the host patched (shared kernel = shared fate), and treat registries like software supply chain (private registry, signed images).

Kubernetes (K8s): the orchestrator - schedules containers across nodes, self-heals, scales, rolling updates. Concepts: Pod (smallest unit), Deployment, Service (stable networking), Ingress, ConfigMap/Secret. You won't admin K8s day-one in most infra roles, but 'pods vs containers, services for discovery, rolling updates' must be conversational.

Decision framework: VM when you need full OS control, strong isolation, or Windows roles. Container when you need density, speed, reproducibility, and stateless-ish services. Many shops run containers ON VMs - the layers compose.

cards.back: VM: hardware-level, full OS. Container: shared kernel, process-level.
Image: template (layers). Container: running instance. Volume: persistent state.
:latest shifts under you - non-reproducible, risky.
Compile in one stage, ship only artifacts - small, safer images.
Run as root; bake in secrets; use :latest in prod.
Smallest deployable unit - one or more containers sharing network/storage.
Volumes + image definitions/Compose files - not containers.
Multi-container app as one versioned, reproducible file.

choices: They share the host kernel - no guest OS boot
quiz.explain: No OS boot = instant start.

choices: Attach a volume for the data directory
quiz.explain: State must live outside the ephemeral container.

quiz.q: Dockerfile best practice:
choices: Non-root USER, pinned base, .dockerignore, layer order by change frequency
quiz.explain: Least privilege + reproducibility + cache efficiency.

quiz.q: AD domain controller in a container?
choices: No - full OS role needing strong isolation; use a VM
quiz.explain: Wrong tool: DCs need full OS control and isolation.

quiz.q: K8s Service provides:
quiz.explain: Pods die; Services give a stable endpoint.

quiz.q: Shared kernel means:
choices: Host kernel CVE affects all containers - patch the host
quiz.explain: Shared fate - host patching is container security.

quiz.q: Rolling update in K8s:
choices: Replace pods incrementally with zero downtime
quiz.explain: Incremental replacement = always serving.

quiz.q: Your monitoring stack as code:
quiz.explain: Compose = infrastructure as code for services.

modules.title: Azure Fundamentals for Infra Admins
modules.summary: Azure through an infrastructure lens: subscriptions, VNets, VMs, storage, Entra, and what everything costs. You need this for -> M17/M22 and hybrid/cloud interviews.
objectives: Navigate the hierarchy: management groups, subscriptions, resource groups.
Build a VNet with subnets, NSGs, and a VM (portal + CLI).
Choose storage tiers and VM series conversationally.
Estimate costs and name the top cost controls.

notes.title: Hierarchy and identity
notes.body:
Hierarchy: Management Groups -> Subscriptions (billing + policy boundary) -> Resource Groups (lifecycle boundary - delete the group, delete everything) -> Resources. Naming convention + mandatory tags (owner, env, costcenter) from day one - untagged sprawl is the #1 cloud mess.

Entra ID is the identity plane (M17): every Azure action authenticates through it. RBAC: Owner/Contributor/Reader + granular roles, assigned at scope (subscription/RG/resource). PIM (Privileged Identity Management): just-in-time admin elevation - standing admin rights are the old way.

Policy: guardrails as code (allowed regions, required tags, VM SKUs). Blueprints/landing zones package the standard. An infra admin who says 'policy enforces our tagging and region rules' speaks cloud governance.

notes.title: Network and compute
notes.body:
VNet: your cloud network - address space, subnets (separate tiers: web/app/data), NSGs (subnet/NIC firewall rules - the cloud ACL), route tables, peering (VNet-to-VNet). No broadcast domain worries; plan address space to avoid overlap with on-prem (VPN/ExpressRoute needs non-overlapping ranges).

VMs: series (D=general, E=memory, F=compute, N=GPU), sizes, managed disks (Premium SSD for production), availability sets/zones (fault/update domains; zones = datacenter-level). Bastion for RDP/SSH without public IPs; JIT access narrows exposure.

Hybrid: Site-to-Site VPN (encrypted over internet) vs ExpressRoute (private circuit - consistent latency, more money). Azure Arc extends management to on-prem servers (policy, updates, inventory) - the hybrid admin's bridge.

notes.title: Storage, backup, and the money
notes.body:
Storage accounts: Blob (object), Files (SMB shares!), Disks, Tables/Queues. Tiers: Hot/Cool/Cold/Archive - lifecycle policies move data down automatically. Azure Files can literally replace a file server with AD-authenticated SMB shares.

Backup: Azure Backup (VMs, files, SQL) with vaults and retention policies; Site Recovery for DR failover (the cloud M31). Monitor: Log Analytics + alerts - the M33 concepts, cloud-native.

Cost: pay-as-you-go per second; the bill shock comes from: oversized VMs, unattached disks, forgotten test RGs, data egress. modules.title: AWS Fundamentals for Infra Admins
modules.summary: AWS through the same infrastructure lens: VPCs, EC2, storage, IAM, and cost. Multi-cloud literacy doubles your interview surface. You need this for -> cloud conversations and M31/M33.
objectives: Build a VPC with public/private subnets, IGW, NAT, and security groups.
Launch and operate EC2 instances (AMIs, instance types, EBS).

Apply IAM least privilege (users, roles, policies, MFA).

notes.title: VPC: your cloud datacenter
notes.body:
VPC = isolated network: CIDR block, subnets across Availability Zones (AZs - separate datacenters). Public subnets route to an Internet Gateway; private subnets reach the internet via NAT Gateway (outbound only). Route tables steer; Network ACLs (stateless, subnet-level) + Security Groups (stateful, instance-level) filter - SGs are the ones you touch daily.

AZ design: spread across 2-3 AZs for resilience; each AZ is isolated power/cooling/network. Regions for geography/compliance. Non-overlapping CIDRs with on-prem for VPN/Direct Connect - same rule as Azure.

VPC peering / Transit Gateway connect VPCs; VPN or Direct Connect (the ExpressRoute equivalent) bridges on-prem. Default VPC exists - don't build production in it; build your own with intention.

notes.title: EC2, storage, and IAM
notes.body:
EC2: AMIs (golden images - build your own hardened ones), instance types (t=burstable, m=general, c=compute, r=memory, g=GPU), EBS volumes (gp3 general, io2 critical; snapshots for backup), key pairs for SSH (guard the .pem like a password), user data for bootstrap scripts.

S3: object storage - buckets, versioning, encryption, storage classes (Standard/IA/Glacier), lifecycle policies to Glacier. EFS (managed NFS) and FSx (Windows file shares!) for file workloads.

IAM: users (humans), roles (for services/instances - EC2 instance profiles, never access keys on instances), policies (JSON least-privilege), MFA everywhere, no root key usage. IAM is the FIRST thing to get right - most AWS breaches are IAM mistakes, not AWS mistakes.

notes.title: Shared responsibility and cost
notes.body:
Shared responsibility: AWS secures OF the cloud (hardware, hypervisor, facilities); you secure IN the cloud (your data, IAM, OS patching, SG rules, encryption). Saying this correctly in an interview signals cloud maturity.

Cost: per-second EC2, S3 per-GB, data transfer out. Surprises: NAT Gateway hourly + per-GB, forgotten EBS snapshots, cross-AZ traffic. Controls: Budgets + Cost Anomaly alerts, Compute Optimizer right-sizing, Savings Plans / Reserved Instances, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, Instance Scheduler for dev.

Multi-cloud reality: most orgs are Azure-primary or AWS-primary with the other for specific workloads. Your value: the patterns transfer (VNet=VPC, NSG=SG, Bastion=Session Manager). Learn one deeply, map the other.

modules.title: OS Imaging & Deployment
modules.summary: Deploy Windows at scale: golden images, MDT, Sysprep, PXE boot, and Autopilot. The skill behind every 'new hire laptop ready' story. You need this for -> M24/M25 and fleet onboarding.
objectives: Build a sysprepped golden image and explain the generalize step.
Run an MDT deployment share: task sequences, drivers, applications.
Explain the PXE boot chain and its DHCP/DNS dependencies.
Compare imaging vs Autopilot/Intune provisioning.
Troubleshoot failed deployments via logs (BDD.log, SMSTS.log).

notes.title: Golden images and Sysprep
notes.body:
Golden image: a reference Windows install (updates, baseline apps, settings) captured to a WIM file, then deployed to fleets. The critical step: Sysprep /generalize - strips machine identity (SID, GUID, drivers) so clones don't collide. Skip it and you get duplicate SIDs, WSUS ID collisions, and KMS chaos.

Build the reference VM (never on physical hardware - driver pollution), snapshot, sysprep, capture with DISM. Thin vs thick vs hybrid images: thin (vanilla OS + apps installed at deploy - flexible, slower), thick (everything baked - fast, brittle), hybrid (OS + core apps baked, the rest at deploy - the sweet spot).

Modern shift: Microsoft pushes away from imaging toward cloud provisioning (Autopilot) - but imaging still rules for labs, specialized hardware, and offline builds. Know both; lead with the future.

notes.title: MDT: the free deployment workhorse
notes.body:
Microsoft Deployment Toolkit (MDT): free, powerful, the classic. Components: Deployment Share (the repository), Task Sequences (the recipe: partition, apply image, inject drivers, install apps, join domain), boot images (WinPE - the mini-OS that starts it all), and the rules (CustomSettings.ini - ZeroTouch vs LiteTouch).

Driver management: total control method (driver per model via WMI query) - import once, inject by model, never 'one driver pack for all'. Applications: silent installs (/quiet /norestart - test every installer manually first). The task sequence is code: version it, test changes on one model, then fleet.

PXE chain (M14's options in action): PXE boot -> DHCP (IP + options 066/067) -> TFTP downloads WinPE boot image -> WinPE connects to deployment share -> task sequence runs. WDS (Windows Deployment Services) serves the PXE/TFTP side; MDT handles the logic.

notes.title: Autopilot and modern provisioning
notes.body:
Windows Autopilot: cloud provisioning - the device ships from the OEM (or gets a hardware hash imported), user signs in, Intune pushes config/apps/policies. No imaging, no PXE, no on-prem infrastructure. Profiles: user-driven (employee sets up) vs self-deploying (kiosk/shared).

When each wins: Autopilot for cloud-managed fleets and remote workers (zero-touch, anywhere); MDT/imaging for specialized hardware, labs, offline/air-gapped builds, and full OS customization. Hybrid reality: many orgs image the tricky 10% and Autopilot the rest.

Troubleshooting: MDT -> BDD.log (the master log) and SMSTS.log (task sequence); PXE failures -> DHCP options/IP helpers; Autopilot -> Intune enrollment status, ESP (Enrollment Status Page) blocks, hardware hash import. 'It worked on this model but not that one' is always drivers - total control method exists for exactly this.

cards.back: Strips machine identity (SID, GUID) so clones don't collide.

cards.front: Thin vs thick vs hybrid images
cards.back: Thin: vanilla+apps at deploy. Thick: all baked. Hybrid: OS+core baked (sweet spot).
The deployment recipe: partition, image, drivers, apps, domain join.
DHCP (066/067) -> TFTP WinPE -> deployment share -> task sequence.
Total control: per-model injection via WMI query.

modules.title: Patch Management Strategy
modules.summary: The discipline that stops most breaches: rings, cadences, WSUS/Intune mechanics, emergency lanes, and rollback. Interview-critical - 'how do you patch' reveals seniority. You need this for -> M32/M37.
objectives: Design ring-based rollout (pilot/broad/critical) with timelines.
Operate the monthly cadence: Patch Tuesday through deadline.
Run the emergency out-of-band process for zero-days.
Measure compliance: reporting, SLAs, and exception handling.
Explain rollback options when a patch breaks something.

notes.title: Rings and cadence
notes.body:
Rings: Pilot (IT + volunteers, day 1-3 - find the breakage), Broad (most of fleet, day 4-10), Critical (servers/Execs, day 11-14 with maintenance windows). Deadlines force installation; grace periods respect user work. No ring skips: even 'urgent' patches ride the emergency lane, not a shortcut.

Monthly cadence: Patch Tuesday (second Tuesday) -> sync metadata -> pilot approvals -> monitor pilot 48-72h -> broad approvals -> deadline enforcement -> compliance report. Servers get their own windows (never 'reboot whenever' - cluster-aware updating for Hyper-V hosts, maintenance mode for app servers).

Third-party patching (browsers, Adobe, Java, drivers) is where most fleets actually bleed - WSUS doesn't cover it; Intune/third-party tools do. A 'fully patched' Windows fleet with 2-year-old Chrome is not patched.

notes.title: Tooling: WSUS, Intune, and the mix
notes.body:
WSUS (M15): on-prem, free, GPO-driven - approvals per group, deadlines, reporting. Great for traditional domains; weak on remote workers and third-party apps. Intune/Windows Update for Business: cloud policy - rings, deadlines, feature-update deferrals; reaches anywhere with internet; Autopatch (Microsoft-managed) for hands-off.

Most real orgs: hybrid - WSUS or Intune for OS, a third-party tool (or Intune) for apps, and manual processes for firmware/network gear (switches, iDRAC, UPS - the forgotten patch surface). Document the matrix: system type -> tool -> cadence -> owner.

Compliance reporting: % patched within SLA per ring, mean-time-to-patch for criticals, exception list with expirations. 'We're 98% compliant on criticals within 14 days' is the sentence leadership wants.

notes.title: Emergencies and rollbacks
notes.body:
Zero-day lane: assess (is it exploitable in our environment?) -> pilot fast (hours, not days) -> broad within 24-48h -> emergency deadline -> verify. Pre-authorized: the emergency lane needs standing approval, or you'll debate while attackers work. Communication template ready: what, who, when, action required.

Rollback: Windows allows uninstalling most updates (wusa /uninstall /kb), Known Issue Rollback (KIR) via GPO for Microsoft-pushed fixes, and system restore/checkpoints for the brave. Test restores before you need them. Some updates can't roll back (servicing stack) - that's what the pilot ring is for.

Exceptions: documented, time-bound, risk-accepted (that legacy app that breaks on .NET updates). Review quarterly. An exception without an expiry is just negligence with paperwork.

modules.title: MDM & Intune Concepts
modules.summary: Modern device management: Intune enrollment, compliance, configuration profiles, and Autopilot's partner. You need this for -> M23/M28 and every modern endpoint conversation.
objectives: Compare GPO vs Intune management and know when each applies.
Enroll devices (Autopilot, bulk, BYOD) and explain the profiles.

Deploy apps and updates via Intune.
Troubleshoot enrollment and policy failures.

notes.title: The management plane shift
notes.body:
GPO: on-prem, domain-joined, LAN-centric, 20 years of power. Intune: cloud, internet-centric, MDM protocol (OMA-DM) + MAM for apps. Co-management (ConfigMgr + Intune): the bridge - workloads (compliance, apps, updates) slide from on-prem to cloud one by one.

Enrollment: Autopilot (zero-touch, M23), bulk enrollment packages, BYOD (work profile / MAM without full enrollment). Enrollment IS the trust moment - device identity + compliance attestation begins here. A device that can't enroll can't be trusted, full stop.

Profiles vs policies: Configuration profiles (settings - like GPO), Compliance policies (rules: encryption on, OS version, jailbreak detection), App deployment (required/available/uninstall). Assignment by Entra groups - dynamic groups (all Windows 11 laptops) do the targeting work.

notes.title: Compliance as the Zero Trust signal
notes.body:
Compliance policy: the device health checklist - BitLocker on, Defender active, OS patched, no jailbreak, password complexity. Noncompliant -> Conditional Access blocks corporate apps (M17's engine consuming Intune's signal). This is Zero Trust in action: access decisions from live device posture, not network location.

Remediation: auto-remediate where possible (require encryption -> Intune can trigger it), notify the user with grace periods, then block. The user experience matters: 'your device needs an update to access email' beats a silent block.

Monitoring: per-device compliance state, policy assignment status, enrollment errors. Intune's 'what if' equivalent: test assignments on pilot groups. A compliance policy typo can block the CEO's email - pilot everything.

notes.title: Apps, updates, and troubleshooting
notes.body:
App deployment: Win32 apps (wrapped with the prep tool), Microsoft 365 apps, Store apps, required (auto-install) vs available (company portal). Dependencies and supersedence chain versions properly. Update rings (M24's rings, cloud edition): feature update deferrals, quality update deadlines.

Troubleshooting: enrollment failures -> check Entra join state, MDM authority, licenses (Intune license required!); policy not applying -> assignment, group membership, sync (manual sync from Company Portal), conflicting profiles (Intune shows conflicts explicitly); app install fail -> wrapped correctly? detection rules? logs on device.

The interview line: 'Intune is how I manage devices that never touch the LAN; GPO is how I manage the ones that live on it; co-management is the migration path.'

modules.title: Endpoint Hardening Checklists (CIS-Concept)
modules.summary: Harden Windows endpoints systematically: CIS Benchmark concepts, baselines, LAPS, BitLocker, Defender. Interview-critical - hardening is a core ThreatLocker-adjacent skill. You need this for -> M27/M28/M32.
objectives: Apply CIS Benchmark concepts via baselines and GPO/Intune.
Deploy LAPS for local admin password management.

notes.title: Baselines: CIS Benchmarks in practice
notes.body:
CIS Benchmarks: consensus hardening guides (Level 1 = safe for most, Level 2 = high security, some breakage risk). You don't memorize 300 settings - you apply the benchmark via GPO/Intune baseline, test on pilot, handle exceptions. Microsoft's Security Baselines (built into Intune/GPO) are the equivalent starting point.

The workflow: import baseline -> compare against current (what changes?) -> pilot -> exceptions documented -> deploy -> monitor drift (compliance policies re-check). 'We hardened to CIS L1 with 12 documented exceptions' is audit-ready language.

Key settings families: password/lockout (via AD), audit policy (logon events, privilege use), user rights (who can do what), security options (guest, autorun, LLMNR - disable the legacy protocols attackers love), Defender, firewall, BitLocker.

notes.title: LAPS, BitLocker, and local attack surface
notes.body:
LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution / Windows LAPS now built-in): unique random local admin password per machine, rotated, stored in AD/Entra. Kills lateral movement via shared local passwords - one of the highest-ROI hardening moves that exists.

BitLocker: full-disk encryption - TPM + PIN for pre-boot auth on sensitive machines; recovery keys escrowed to AD/Entra (a BitLockered laptop with the key only in the user's head is a data-loss incident). Verify with compliance policy; the M25 signal feeds access decisions.

Local attack surface: disable LLMNR/NBT-NS (poisoning attacks), SMBv1 (WannaCry's vector - gone in modern Windows), Autorun, guest account, and unnecessary services. Each disabled legacy protocol is a closed attacker door.

notes.title: Defender and the hardening loop
notes.body:
Microsoft Defender: AV + EDR sensor in one. ASR rules (Attack Surface Reduction): block Office macros from internet, block credential stealing from LSASS, block process injection - each rule in audit mode first (what WOULD break?), then block. Controlled folder access vs ransomware.

Hardening loop: baseline -> deploy -> monitor (Defender Secure Score, compliance) -> drift remediation -> re-baseline. Secure Score is gamified but directionally useful. Vulnerability management (Defender) shows exposed CVEs per device - feed it into M24's patching.

The checklist (your deliverable): per device type (laptop/desktop/server/kiosk), the settings, the enforcement method (GPO/Intune), the verification (compliance), and the exception process. A hardening checklist that isn't measured is a wish list.

cards.back: L1: safe for most. L2: high security, some breakage risk.
Shared local admin passwords -> unique, rotated, escrowed per machine.
Recovery keys to AD/Entra - never only in someone's head.
Audit mode first (measure breakage), then block.
LLMNR/NBT-NS, SMBv1, Autorun, Guest.
Baseline -> deploy -> monitor drift -> remediate -> re-baseline.
Directionally useful gamification - not a security guarantee.
A wish list - enforce via GPO/Intune, verify via compliance.

modules.title: Application Control & Allowlisting Concepts
modules.summary: Default-deny for executables: AppLocker, WDAC, and the allowlisting mindset behind ThreatLocker's world. Interview-critical. You need this for -> M28 and the Zero Trust story.
objectives: Explain allowlisting vs blocklisting and why default-deny wins.
Design AppLocker rules (publisher/path/hash) and rollout stages.
Describe WDAC (Device Guard) and when it supersedes AppLocker.
Run the audit-then-enforce rollout without breaking the business.
Connect allowlisting to the Zero Trust narrative.

notes.title: The default-deny mindset
notes.body:
Blocklisting (antivirus model): allow everything except known-bad. Allowlisting: deny everything except known-good. The math: malware variants are infinite; your approved app catalog is finite. Default-deny is the only model that handles unknown threats - which is why it's a Zero Trust pillar and the core of companies built on allowlisting.

Independent framing: this course teaches the CONCEPT and the built-in Windows tools. Commercial products (including ThreatLocker's) productize this with central management, but the principle and the rollout discipline are tool-agnostic - and that's what interviews test.

Where it applies: fixed-function devices first (kiosks, POS, lab machines), then servers (predictable workloads), then knowledge-worker fleets (hardest - app sprawl). Start where the app catalog is smallest.

notes.title: AppLocker: the built-in workhorse
notes.body:
AppLocker (Enterprise/Education): rules for executables, scripts, installers, packaged apps. Rule types: Publisher (signed, version-flexible - the maintainable choice), Path (simple, bypassable by file moves), Hash (exact binary - brittle, breaks on updates). Default rules first (allow Windows + Program Files), then your allow rules.

Rollout: Audit mode (log what WOULD block - Event Log) -> analyze (which legit apps hit?) -> build rules -> enforce on pilot -> fleet. The audit phase is non-negotiable: enforcing blind breaks the business on day one. Exceptions via rule collections per OU/group.

Maintenance: publisher rules survive updates (version ranges); new apps need rule requests (the ticketing workflow - M04's process applied). Users requesting software becomes a governed pipeline, not a hallway conversation.

notes.title: WDAC and the enterprise picture
notes.body:
WDAC (Windows Defender Application Control, formerly Device Guard): kernel-level enforcement, stronger than AppLocker (which is user-mode and bypassable by admins). Policy in signed XML; can require HVCI (memory integrity). Use WDAC where tamper-resistance matters: servers, high-security endpoints.

Managed Installer / Intelligent Security Graph: trust apps deployed by your management tool (Intune) automatically - the modern answer to 'how do we allow without whitelisting every binary'. Combined with reputation-based rules, this scales allowlisting to real fleets.

The interview narrative: 'Allowlisting is default-deny for code. I start with audit mode to map the real app catalog, roll out publisher rules by device tier, and maintain it as a governed request pipeline. It's the endpoint enforcement of Zero Trust - every execution is an access decision.'

cards.back: Allow: deny-all-except-approved. Block: allow-all-except-known-bad. Default-deny handles unknowns.
Publisher (maintainable) > Path (simple, bypassable) > Hash (brittle).
Audit -> analyze -> rules -> pilot enforce -> fleet.
WDAC: kernel-level, tamper-resistant. AppLocker: user-mode, easier, bypassable by admins.
Fixed-function devices -> servers -> knowledge workers (easiest catalog first).
Auto-trust apps deployed by your management tool.
Allow Windows/Program Files or you brick the OS on enforcement.
A governed ticket pipeline, not hallway conversation.

choices: Default-deny blocks unknown code; blocklists only know known-bad
quiz.explain: Unknown threats are the gap blocklists can't cover.

choices: Business breakage day one - legit apps blocked
quiz.explain: Audit maps the real catalog first - non-negotiable.

quiz.q: Rule for an app that updates monthly. Best type?
quiz.explain: Publisher rules survive updates; hash rules break.

quiz.q: Server needs tamper-resistant enforcement. Choose?
quiz.explain: Kernel enforcement resists admin bypass.

quiz.q: First allowlisting target in a hospital?
quiz.explain: Smallest catalog, clearest win, then expand.

quiz.q: User needs a new app under allowlisting. Process?
quiz.explain: The pipeline keeps default-deny intact.

quiz.q: Managed Installer / ISG helps by:
choices: Auto-trusting apps from your management tools
quiz.explain: Scales allow decisions via trusted deployment.

quiz.q: Allowlisting's Zero Trust connection:
choices: Every execution is an access decision - verify per binary
quiz.explain: Default-deny execution = Zero Trust at the endpoint.

modules.title: Zero Trust Architecture Principles
modules.summary: The strategy behind the job title: NIST SP 800-207 tenets, CISA maturity model, and applying Zero Trust to real infrastructure. Interview-critical - this is the company's language. You need this for -> M29/M30 and every interview answer.
objectives: State the NIST SP 800-207 tenets and apply each to infrastructure.
Place an org on the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model (Traditional/Initial/Advanced/Optimal).
Design identity, device, and network controls per Zero Trust.
Explain what Zero Trust does NOT mean (no product, no rip-and-replace).
Answer 'what is Zero Trust' in 60 seconds, 5 minutes, and 30 minutes.

notes.title: NIST SP 800-207: the tenets
notes.body:
Zero Trust = 'never trust, always verify' applied to every access decision. NIST SP 800-207 (the authoritative definition - read it, it's public) tenets: (1) All data sources and computing services are resources. (2) All communication is secured. (3) Access to individual resources is granted per-session. (4) Access is determined by dynamic policy (identity, device, behavior). (5) The enterprise monitors the integrity and security posture of all assets. (6) Authentication/authorization are dynamic and strictly enforced before access. (7) The enterprise collects as much information as possible to improve posture.

Key shift: identity becomes the perimeter. Network location stops being a trust signal - a domain-joined laptop on the LAN gets the same verification as one at a coffee shop. For infrastructure teams this means: every service needs identity-aware access, every device needs health attestation, every flow needs policy.

What it's NOT: not a product you buy, not 'no VPN', not rip-and-replace. It's an architecture you migrate toward - microsegmentation, strong identity, device compliance, least privilege - each a project, each valuable alone.

notes.title: CISA maturity model: where are we?
notes.body:
CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model: 5 pillars (Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications, Data) × 3 cross-cutting (Visibility/Analytics, Automation/Orchestration, Governance) across 4 stages: Traditional -> Initial -> Advanced -> Optimal. Use it to ASSESS, not to impress: 'our identity is Advanced (phishing-resistant MFA, Conditional Access), our networks are Initial (flat VLANs, no microsegmentation)'.

Typical enterprise reality: Identity leads (MFA, CA), Devices follow (Intune compliance), Networks lag (flat networks are everywhere), Data trails (classification is hard). Your infrastructure roadmap IS the maturity climb: each M28-M33 module moves a pillar.

Interview power: walking in with 'here's how I'd assess your maturity and the first three projects I'd run' turns a Q&A into a working session. Assess honestly - claiming Optimal anything invites hard questions.

notes.title: Applying it: the infrastructure playbook
notes.body:
Identity: phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/Windows Hello), Conditional Access everywhere, no standing admin rights (PIM/JIT). Devices: compliance-gated access (M25), allowlisting on fixed functions (M27), EDR everywhere. Networks: microsegment (M29), private access over VPN-sprawl, DNS-layer policy. Applications: SSO everything, kill legacy auth. Data: classify, encrypt, DLP on the crown jewels.

The 60-second answer: 'Zero Trust means every access decision verifies identity, device health, and context - no implicit trust from network location. Practically: strong MFA, compliant devices, microsegmentation, and least-privilege access, measured against the CISA maturity model.'

The 30-minute version adds: your assessment of THEIR maturity, the project sequence (identity first - cheapest wins), metrics (MFA coverage %, compliant device %, segmented workloads), and honest scope ('this is a multi-year architecture, not a product install').

cards.back: Never trust, always verify - every access decision checks identity, device, context.

cards.front: NIST SP 800-207 tenet count + core idea
cards.back: 7 tenets; identity is the perimeter, access per-session by dynamic policy.
Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications, Data (+ visibility, automation, governance).
Traditional -> Initial -> Advanced -> Optimal.
Identity -> Devices -> Networks -> Data.
A product, 'no VPN', or rip-and-replace - it's an architecture you migrate toward.

cards.front: First project in a ZT rollout
cards.back: Identity: phishing-resistant MFA + Conditional Access (cheapest wins).
MFA coverage %, compliant devices %, segmented workloads, legacy auth blocked.

quiz.explain: No product confers Zero Trust; it's designed and measured.

quiz.explain: Identity and device health decide, not network location.

choices: Each resource access is authorized individually - no broad network trust
quiz.explain: Granular, per-resource authorization.

quiz.q: Dynamic policy (tenet 4) uses:
quiz.explain: Multiple live signals drive each decision.

quiz.explain: Identity controls are high-ROI and fast.

quiz.q: 'We have Zero Trust because we removed VPN.' Problem?
choices: Removing VPN isn't Zero Trust - verification architecture is
quiz.explain: Zero Trust is what replaces implicit trust, not one tool removal.

quiz.q: Governance cross-cutting capability means:
choices: Policies, risk management, and compliance overseeing all pillars
quiz.explain: Governance steers the whole program.

modules.title: Microsegmentation & Network Access Control
modules.summary: Shrink the blast radius: VLAN/ACL segmentation, host firewalls, 802.1X/NAC, and lateral-movement defense. Interview-critical - segmentation is where infrastructure meets Zero Trust. You need this for -> M28/M30.
objectives: Design a segmented network (tiers, VLANs, ACLs) and justify each boundary.
Explain east-west vs north-south traffic and why east-west matters.
Deploy 802.1X concepts: supplicant, authenticator, RADIUS/NPS.
Use Windows Firewall with Advanced Security as a segmentation tool.
Detect and respond to lateral movement patterns.

notes.title: Segmentation design
notes.body:
Flat network = one compromised host reaches everything (the ransomware dream). Segmentation draws boundaries: user VLANs, server VLANs, management VLAN, DMZ, IoT/printer VLAN, guest. Between them: ACLs or firewall policy - default deny, allow only required flows.

East-west (server-to-server, host-to-host) is where lateral movement lives - and where most orgs have ZERO inspection. North-south (in/out of the datacenter) gets the firewall love. Microsegmentation pushes policy to the workload/host itself (host firewall rules per role) - the network equivalent of allowlisting.

Design method: map required flows first (app->DB:1433, users->app:443, admins->mgmt:3389/22), then write allow rules for exactly those, deny the rest. Document each rule's owner and purpose - undocumented firewall rules are how 'temporary' becomes permanent.

notes.title: NAC and 802.1X
notes.body:
NAC answers 'should this device be on my network at all?' 802.1X: port-based authentication - supplicant (device) -> authenticator (switch/AP) -> authentication server (RADIUS/NPS talking to AD). Success = VLAN assignment by policy (employees->corp VLAN, printers->printer VLAN, unknowns->quarantine).

RADIUS/NPS on Windows Server: policies by group, device type, health (with NAP remnants or modern compliance checks). MAB (MAC auth bypass) for dumb devices (printers, cameras) - MAC allowlist, weak but better than open ports.

Reality check: full 802.1X is a project (certificates, switch config, exception handling). Start with: DHCP snooping + DAI on switches (kills basic spoofing), guest isolation, and a plan. NAC maturity climbs with the org.

notes.title: Host firewalls and lateral defense
notes.body:
Windows Firewall with Advanced Security: per-profile (domain/private/public), per-rule (program/port/IP scope), manageable by GPO at fleet scale. The microsegmentation workhorse: servers allow only their role's ports from only their tier's subnets. 'Allow SQL 1433 from app-tier only' beats any VLAN alone.

Lateral movement patterns to know: SMB/PSExec hopping, RDP jumps, WMI, credential dumping (LSASS), pass-the-hash. Defenses layer: LAPS (M26 - no shared creds), Credential Guard, network segmentation (this module), EDR (M32), and log correlation (M33's SIEM feeds).

Test it: from a lab workstation, try to reach a 'server' on another VLAN - verify the deny, check the firewall log, then add the allow rule and verify. Segmentation you haven't tested is decoration.

cards.back: East-west: host-to-host (lateral movement). North-south: in/out of DC.
Policy at the workload/host level - network allowlisting.
Supplicant (device) -> authenticator (switch) -> RADIUS server.
Dumb devices (printers/cameras) - MAC-based, weak but better than open.
Domain, Private, Public - different rule sets per network.
DHCP snooping + DAI, guest isolation, tier VLANs with ACLs.
SMB/PSExec, RDP, WMI, LSASS dumping, pass-the-hash.
Permanent - document owner and purpose per rule.

quiz.explain: Lateral movement needs lateral controls.

choices: Quarantine VLAN or no access until authenticated
quiz.explain: Port-level auth gates network entry.

choices: MAB (MAC bypass) on a dedicated printer VLAN
quiz.explain: Weak auth + isolated VLAN = pragmatic.

quiz.q: App server should take SQL only from app tier. Implement?
choices: Host firewall rule: 1433 from app-tier subnet only
quiz.explain: Workload-level policy = microsegmentation.

quiz.q: DHCP snooping + DAI prevent:
choices: Rogue DHCP and ARP spoofing on the LAN
quiz.explain: Switch-level anti-spoofing basics.

quiz.q: Design order for firewall rules:
choices: Map required flows first, then allow-list them, deny rest
quiz.explain: Flows drive rules; documentation per rule.

quiz.q: Guest Wi-Fi design must include:
choices: Isolation from corp + captive portal + rate limits
quiz.explain: Guests get internet, nothing else.

quiz.q: You haven't tested a segment boundary. It is:
quiz.explain: Test every boundary both ways.

modules.title: Incident Response for Infrastructure Teams
modules.summary: When security calls at 2 AM: containment, evidence, eradication, recovery - the infrastructure role in IR. Interview-critical - IR stories are STAR gold. You need this for -> M31/M32 and on-call readiness.
objectives: Execute the IR lifecycle: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, lessons.
Perform first-responder actions: isolate, preserve evidence, capture memory.
Explain the infrastructure admin's role vs the SOC's role.
Write an incident report and run a blameless postmortem.
Build a jump kit and call tree before you need them.

notes.title: The lifecycle and your role
notes.body:
NIST 800-61 lifecycle: Preparation -> Detection & Analysis -> Containment/Eradication/Recovery -> Post-Incident. The SOC detects and analyzes; INFRASTRUCTURE contains and recovers: isolate hosts (network, not power - memory evidence dies with power), disable accounts, block at firewall, snapshot before rebuild, restore from known-good.

First responder rules: don't log into the compromised box with domain admin (credential theft), don't 'clean and reboot' before evidence (you destroy the timeline), DO isolate (pull the network cable / disable switch port / EDR isolate), photograph the screen, note the time, escalate per the call tree.

Containment choices: short-term (isolate host, block IP) vs long-term (rebuild, reimage, credential reset fleet-wide if domain compromise suspected). Ransomware: isolate first, identify variant, check backups BEFORE negotiating anything - and know your org's ransom policy in advance.

notes.title: Evidence and eradication
notes.body:
Evidence basics for infra: memory capture (before reboot!), disk image or snapshot, firewall/proxy logs, AD logs (4624/4625/4768), EDR timeline. Chain of custody: who touched what, when - a shared doc started at minute one. You don't need to be a forensics expert; you need to PRESERVE so experts can work.

Eradication: find the root cause (patient zero, entry vector), remove persistence (scheduled tasks, services, WMI, registry run keys), close the vector (patch, config, phish training). Rebuilding from known-good media beats 'cleaning' - assume the box is untrustworthy until rebuilt.

Recovery: restore in priority order (identity first - DCs, then core services, then users), verify clean (scan restored data), monitor for re-infection. Communicate: who needs to know what, when - the comms plan is part of preparation, not improvisation.

notes.title: Preparation: the jump kit
notes.body:
Jump kit (have it BEFORE the incident): clean USBs with tools (memory capture, AV scanners), known-good ISOs, credential reset scripts, network diagrams, asset inventory, call tree (who, in what order, with phone numbers that work at 2 AM), runbooks for the top 5 scenarios (ransomware, BEC, data theft, insider, outage-vs-attack).

Tabletop exercises: walk through a scenario quarterly ('ransomware on the file server, go'). The first time you meet your IR team shouldn't be during the incident. Document decisions and gaps after each exercise.

Postmortem: blameless, timeline-based, action items with owners and dates. 'Human error' is never the root cause - ask why the system allowed it. The report: executive summary (impact, duration), timeline, root cause, actions taken, lessons, improvements. This document is career capital - it proves you operate under pressure.

cards.back: Prepare -> Detect/Analyze -> Contain/Eradicate/Recover -> Post-incident.
SOC: detect/analyze. Infra: contain/recover (isolate, snapshot, rebuild, restore).
Network isolation (cable/port/EDR) - NOT power off (kills memory evidence).

cards.front: Never log into a compromised box with
cards.back: Domain admin - credential theft risk. Use dedicated IR creds.
Rebuild from known-good beats cleaning - assume untrustworthy.
Clean tools USB, ISOs, reset scripts, diagrams, inventory, call tree, runbooks.
Never - ask why the system allowed it.

quiz.q: Ransomware on a file server, 2 AM. First 3 actions?
choices: Isolate (network), preserve evidence (photo/time), escalate per call tree
quiz.explain: Contain, preserve, escalate - in that order.

quiz.q: Why not power off the compromised host?
choices: Memory evidence (running malware, keys) dies with power
quiz.explain: Volatile evidence first.

quiz.q: SOC says 'we need the host isolated'. You:
choices: EDR isolate / disable switch port / pull cable - network, not power
quiz.explain: Network isolation preserves the host for forensics.

quiz.q: Domain admin creds were on the compromised box. Now?
choices: Assume domain compromise: reset KRBTGT twice, reset creds, rebuild DCs if needed
quiz.explain: Credential theft = domain-wide response.

quiz.q: Eradication means:
choices: Remove persistence + close the entry vector, verified
quiz.explain: Root cause gone, vector closed, verified clean.

quiz.q: Postmortem rule #1:
quiz.explain: Blame kills honesty; systems thinking fixes recurrence.

quiz.q: Tabletop exercises are for:
choices: Practicing decisions before the real incident
quiz.explain: Reps before game day.

quiz.q: Recovery priority order?
quiz.explain: Everything authenticates against identity.

modules.title: Backup & Disaster Recovery
modules.summary: The last line of defense: 3-2-1, RPO/RTO, backup types, restore testing, and DR planning. Untested backups are wishes. You need this for -> M30/M34 and business continuity.
objectives: Design 3-2-1 backup architecture with RPO/RTO targets.
Choose full/incremental/differential and retention (GFS).
Protect against ransomware: immutable/air-gapped copies.
Test restores on a schedule and document results.
Write a DR plan with roles, priorities, and communication.

notes.title: 3-2-1 and the objectives
notes.body:
3-2-1: 3 copies of data, 2 different media, 1 offsite. Modern addendum: 1 immutable/air-gapped (ransomware encrypts your online backups too). RPO (how much data can we lose - backup frequency) and RTO (how long to restore - restore speed + process) are BUSINESS decisions you implement: 'RPO 4h, RTO 24h for file services' drives the design.

Backup types: Full (everything - slow, simple restore), Incremental (changes since last backup of any type - fast backup, slow multi-step restore), Differential (changes since last full - middle ground). GFS retention: Grandfather-Father-Son (daily/weekly/monthly) - keep dailies 2 weeks, weeklies 2 months, monthlies a year (adjust to compliance).

What people forget: system state/AD backups (authoritative restore knowledge), configs (firewall, switch, GPO backups), cloud data (M365 needs third-party backup - Microsoft's retention isn't backup), and credentials to access the backups (documented, sealed, tested).

notes.title: Ransomware-proofing backups
notes.body:
Ransomware hunts backups first: mapped drives, backup server creds, cloud buckets. Defenses: immutable storage (S3 Object Lock, immutable vaults - can't be deleted even by admin for the retention period), air-gapped/offline copies (tape, rotated USBs - old school, still works), separate backup credentials (backup admin accounts NOT domain admins), and network isolation of the backup server.

Test the restore, not the backup: 'backup succeeded' emails mean nothing. Quarterly: full restore of a critical system to isolated network, verify boot + data + app. Annual: full DR test. Document results - auditors and insurers ask.

Monitoring: backup job success/failure (alert on failure, obviously), capacity trends, and restore-test calendar. A backup admin's worst day is discovering 6 months of failed jobs during an incident.

notes.title: The DR plan
notes.body:
DR plan structure: objectives (RPO/RTO per tier), roles (who declares disaster, who does what), inventory (what exists, where), priority order (identity -> network -> core apps -> users - M30's order), procedures (step-by-step restores), communication (who tells whom, templates), and test schedule.

Tiers: Tier 1 (hours - identity, core apps), Tier 2 (day - file, print, secondary), Tier 3 (week - nice-to-haves). Cloud DR: Azure Site Recovery / AWS Elastic DR replicate VMs for failover - the M21/M22 concepts applied. On-prem: second site or Hyper-V Replica (M18).

Declaring disaster: who has authority, what's the trigger, where does everyone go (alternate site / remote). Keep a printed copy offsite - the DR plan on the dead file server helps no one.

cards.back: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite, 1 immutable/air-gapped.
RPO: data loss tolerance (frequency). RTO: downtime tolerance (restore speed).
Full: all. Incremental: since any backup. Differential: since last full.
Daily/weekly/monthly tiers - e.g., dailies 2wk, weeklies 2mo, monthlies 1yr.
Immutable storage, air-gapped copies, separate creds, isolated backup server.
The RESTORE (quarterly isolated), not just backup success emails.
Identity -> network -> core apps (tiered) -> users.
Printed offsite - not only on the servers that died.

quiz.q: Backups 'succeed' nightly but restore fails. Lesson?
choices: Test restores quarterly - backup success != recoverability
quiz.explain: Recoverability is the only metric that matters.

quiz.q: Ransomware encrypted the backup server too. Missing?
quiz.explain: Backups need their own security architecture.

quiz.q: Business: 'we can lose 4h of data, be down 1 day.' That's:
quiz.explain: RPO=data loss window; RTO=downtime window.

quiz.q: Fast backup, slower multi-step restore:
quiz.explain: Incremental chains need every link to restore.

quiz.q: M365 data protection: Microsoft's retention is:
choices: Not a backup - use third-party backup for M365
quiz.explain: Shared responsibility: your data, your backup.

quiz.q: AD disaster: which backup matters?
quiz.explain: AD recovery needs system state + procedure.

quiz.q: DR test frequency minimum?
choices: Quarterly restore tests, annual full DR test
quiz.explain: Untested plans are fiction.

quiz.q: Backup admin accounts should be:
quiz.explain: Compromised domain admin shouldn't reach backups.

modules.title: Log Management & SIEM Concepts
modules.summary: See everything: Windows event logs, syslog, centralization, and SIEM/SOAR concepts for the infra admin. You need this for -> M30/M33 and detection conversations.
objectives: Read Windows event logs (Security/System/Application) and key event IDs.
Centralize logs: Windows Event Forwarding, syslog, agents.
Explain SIEM concepts: ingestion, parsing, correlation, alerting.
Write a basic detection (KQL/SPL concept) for a suspicious event.
Manage log retention, volume, and cost.

notes.title: Windows logs: the essential IDs
notes.body:
The big three: Security (4624 logon, 4625 failed logon, 4634 logoff, 4672 special privileges, 4720/4728 account/group changes, 4768/4769 Kerberos), System (1074 shutdown/restart, 6008 unexpected shutdown, service failures), Application (app crashes). Sysmon (Sysinternals): process creation with full command line, network connections, driver loads - the EDR-grade telemetry, free.

Audit policy (GPO): enable logon auditing, account management, privilege use, object access for file servers. Without the audit policy, the logs you need don't exist - 'we weren't logging that' is the saddest IR sentence.

PowerShell: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable for fast queries; wevtutil for CLI. Centralize BEFORE you need them: Windows Event Forwarding (WEF - agentless, GPO-driven subscriptions) to a collector, then to SIEM.

notes.title: Centralization and SIEM
notes.body:
Pipeline: sources (servers, firewalls, switches via syslog, EDR) -> collectors/forwarders -> normalization/parsing -> SIEM storage -> correlation/rules -> alerts -> SOAR playbooks. Microsoft Sentinel (M17/IL-06's territory): cloud SIEM+SOAR, KQL queries, playbooks via Logic Apps.

Correlation example: 5 failed logons (4625) + 1 success (4624) + new service installed = brute-force-to-persistence story no single log tells. Rules: threshold, anomaly, watchlist, threat intel matches. Tuning: every rule needs true/false-positive review or analysts drown.

Infra admin's SIEM role: ensure the logs FLOW (agents healthy, forwarders up, time synced - logs with wrong timestamps are useless), know what each system SHOULD log, and be the person who can pull the raw logs when the SOC asks.

notes.title: KQL basics and log hygiene
notes.body:
KQL (Kusto): SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4625 | summarize count() by Account, Computer | where count_ > 10. The pattern: table -> filter -> summarize -> filter. Learn 5 queries cold: failed logons by account, logons by computer, new services, account creations, rare processes (Sysmon).

Log hygiene: retention policy (hot/warm/cold - 90 days searchable, 1 year archive typical; compliance may demand more), volume control (filter noise at the source - debug logs from chatty apps), and cost (SIEM ingestion is priced per GB - the M21 cost lesson again).

Time: NTP everywhere (M11's checklist) - correlation across systems with skewed clocks is fiction. One second of skew is fine; five minutes breaks Kerberos AND your timeline.

cards.back: Logon success / failed logon / special privileges assigned.
Process creation w/ command line, network conns, driver loads - EDR-grade, free.
Windows Event Forwarding - agentless, GPO-driven log centralization.
Sources -> collectors -> parse -> store -> correlate -> alert -> SOAR.
Table | where (filter) | summarize | where - learn 5 queries cold.
Audit policy via GPO before you need the logs.
Ingestion per GB - filter noise at the source.

cards.front: Time sync matters for logs because
cards.back: Correlation across skewed clocks is fiction.

quiz.q: Brute force against RDP. Which events?
quiz.explain: Failed logons -> success = the brute-force signature.

quiz.q: New account created at 3 AM by unknown admin. Event?
quiz.explain: Account creation outside change windows = red flag.

quiz.q: SOC asks for logs from a server; WEF was never configured. Lesson?
choices: Centralize before incidents - agentless WEF via GPO
quiz.explain: Preparation beats scrambling.

quiz.q: KQL: failed logons per account over 10. Write conceptually:
choices: SecurityEvent | where EventID==4625 | summarize count() by Account | where count_>10
quiz.explain: Filter -> aggregate -> threshold.

quiz.q: SIEM bill tripled. First look?
choices: Noisy sources - filter at collection, check debug/verbose logging
quiz.explain: Volume control at the source.

quiz.q: Sysmon vs default Security log:
choices: Sysmon adds command lines, network, hashes - richer process telemetry
quiz.explain: Deploy Sysmon for real detection depth.

quiz.q: Logs show timestamps 5 minutes apart for one incident. Problem?
choices: Clock skew - fix NTP; timeline unreliable
quiz.explain: Correlation needs synchronized clocks.

quiz.q: Alert fires 500 times a day, all benign. You:
choices: Tune the rule (threshold/allowlist) - alert fatigue kills detection
quiz.explain: Every rule needs FP review.

mockTask.explain: Pipeline + query + response + tuning - the full detection story.

modules.title: Vulnerability & Compliance Basics
modules.summary: Find weaknesses before attackers do: scanning, prioritization, remediation SLAs, and speaking compliance. You need this for -> M24/M32 and audit conversations.
objectives: Run a vulnerability scan and interpret results (CVE, CVSS).
Prioritize by exploitability, not just CVSS score.
Drive remediation with SLAs per severity.
Explain common frameworks (NIST CSF, CIS, PCI, HIPAA) at a conversational level.
Prepare for an audit: evidence, not promises.

notes.title: Scanning and scoring
notes.body:
Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/OpenVAS/Defender VM): authenticated scans (with creds - sees patches, configs) beat unauthenticated (sees banners). Scan regularly: weekly for servers, monthly for workstations, after major changes. Credentials for scanning: dedicated least-privilege scan account.

CVE: the vulnerability's ID. CVSS: 0-10 severity score - useful but flawed (a 9.8 nobody can exploit vs a 7.5 with public exploit). EPSS (exploit prediction) + CISA KEV catalog (known exploited - patch THESE first) beat raw CVSS for prioritization.

False positives: scanners flag generously - verify before panicking. Track: new, recurring, remediated, exception. 'We went from 400 criticals to 40' is the trend leadership funds.

notes.title: Remediation as a program
notes.body:
SLAs by severity: critical (KEV) - days; high - 2 weeks; medium - 30 days; low - 90 days or accept. Owners per system (the M04 accountability lesson); the scanner finds, the owner fixes, you track. Exceptions: documented, compensating controls, expiry - same discipline as M24.

Remediation usually = patching (M24's machine), config change (GPO), or decommission (that 2012 server). The vulnerability program and the patch program are siblings - run them together.

Reporting: open by severity/age, MTTR per severity, SLA compliance %, top recurring. One page, monthly, to leadership. Trends beat snapshots.

notes.title: Compliance conversations
notes.body:
Frameworks you'll hear: NIST CSF 2.0 (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover - the lingua franca), CIS Controls (18 prioritized safeguards), PCI DSS (card data - network segmentation + logging heavy), HIPAA (health data - access controls + audit), SOC 2 (vendor trust - auditors love evidence).

Audit prep: evidence, not promises - 'show me' beats 'we do'. Evidence = configs, logs, tickets, reports with dates. Control mapping: one action satisfies many frameworks (MFA covers CIS, PCI, HIPAA, SOC 2).

The infra admin's compliance role: implement the technical controls, produce the evidence, and never lie to an auditor. 'We don't do that yet; here's our plan with dates' beats a confident fiction every time.

cards.back: Authenticated (with creds): sees patches/configs. Unauthenticated: banners only.
Exploitability (KEV/EPSS), not CVSS alone.
Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog - patch these first.
Critical/KEV: days. High: 2wk. Medium: 30d. Low: 90d/accept.
Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
Evidence, not promises - show configs, logs, tickets with dates.
MFA satisfies CIS, PCI, HIPAA, SOC 2 simultaneously.
Lie. 'Not yet; here's our dated plan' beats fiction.

quiz.q: CVSS 9.8 with no exploit vs 7.5 in CISA KEV. Patch first?
choices: The KEV 7.5 - exploited in the wild beats theoretical severity
quiz.explain: Exploitability drives priority.

quiz.q: Scanner flags 400 criticals. First step?
choices: Verify (FP check), prioritize by KEV/exploitability, assign owners with SLAs
quiz.explain: Triage before action.

quiz.q: That 2012 server can't be patched. Options?
choices: Isolate/segment, compensating controls, documented exception, decommission plan
quiz.explain: Manage unpatchable risk explicitly.

quiz.q: Unauthenticated scan shows clean; authenticated shows 50 missing patches. Lesson?
quiz.explain: Credentialed scans see reality.

quiz.q: Auditor asks 'prove MFA is enforced'. You show:
choices: Conditional Access policies + sign-in logs + compliance report
quiz.explain: Policy + logs + report = evidence.

quiz.q: Vulnerability and patch programs relate how?
choices: Siblings: scanner finds, patch program fixes, vuln program tracks
quiz.explain: Run them as one motion.

quiz.q: SLA breach on a critical: you:
choices: Escalate with risk statement and options, not just the miss
quiz.explain: Risk-framed escalation drives decisions.

quiz.q: NIST CSF 'Govern' (new in 2.0) covers:
choices: Risk strategy, oversight, and policy - the management layer
quiz.explain: Governance over all functions.

handsOnLab.title: Vuln Program: scan, prioritize, remediate
handsOnLab.brief: Run a real scan-to-remediation cycle on your lab.
steps: Install OpenVAS (or Nessus Essentials) as a container (M20); scan the lab authenticated.
Export results; triage: verify 5 findings (FP check), map CVEs to KEV.

handsOnLab.checkpoint: You run vulnerability management as a program, not a scan.

choices: Verify findings, prioritize by exploitability (KEV/EPSS) over raw CVSS, SLA per severity, owners assigned, tracked to closure, exceptions documented
mockTask.explain: Risk-based prioritization with accountability.

modules.title: Monitoring with Zabbix, Prometheus & Grafana
modules.summary: See the infrastructure: metrics vs logs, agent monitoring, alerting that respects sleep, and dashboards people actually read. You need this for -> M35/M36 and on-call sanity.
objectives: Compare Zabbix vs Prometheus/Grafana and choose per environment.
Deploy monitoring: agents, exporters, and key metrics per system.
Write alerts with thresholds, hysteresis, and runbook links.
Build Grafana dashboards for the golden signals.
Defeat alert fatigue with routing, silencing, and tuning.

notes.title: The stack: Zabbix vs Prometheus
notes.body:
Zabbix: all-in-one (server, agents, alerting, dashboards) - great for traditional Windows/Linux fleets, auto-discovery, templates per OS/role. Install the agent, apply the template, done. The enterprise workhorse for heterogeneous infra.

Prometheus: metrics pull model - exporters expose /metrics, Prometheus scrapes, PromQL queries, Grafana visualizes, Alertmanager routes. Cloud-native standard; steeper curve, unbeatable flexibility. Windows exporter covers Windows hosts; snmp_exporter covers network gear.

Metrics vs logs vs traces: metrics (numbers over time - CPU, latency), logs (events - M32), traces (request flows). This module is metrics; M32 was logs; together they're observability. Monitor what matters: the USE/RED golden signals (Utilization, Saturation, Errors / Rate, Errors, Duration).

notes.title: What to monitor (per system)
notes.body:
Universal host: CPU, memory, disk space/inodes, disk latency, network errors, uptime, pending reboot, service states, certificate expiry (the classic outage). AD: replication status, SYSVOL health, DC response time, time skew. Network: interface errors/discards, BGP/OSPF state, DHCP scope utilization (M14's 80% alert).

Application: service port responding, synthetic transactions (log in like a user - catches what pings miss), backup job success, queue depths. Cloud: billing alerts (M21), quota usage, instance health checks.

Baselines first: monitor for 2 weeks before alerting on anomalies - 'disk 80% full' alerts on a stable archive server are noise. Every metric needs: why it matters, threshold, who gets paged, and the runbook link.

notes.title: Alerting without the 3 AM burnout
notes.body:
Alert rules: thresholds with hysteresis (alert at 90%, clear at 80% - no flapping), sustained duration (5 min, not 1 spike), severity tiers (page vs ticket vs info). Routing: PagerDuty/Opsgenie schedules, escalation chains, business-hours vs 24/7 per service tier.

Runbook links in every alert: 'what this means, first 3 checks, who to call'. An alert without a runbook is a panic notification. Silencing: maintenance windows auto-silence; acknowledge stops escalation.

Alert fatigue math: if >5 pages/week per person, tune or die - people start ignoring, then miss the real one. Weekly alert review: which fired, were they actionable, tune or delete. Dashboards: one NOC overview (red/green per service), per-team detail, and executive uptime. A dashboard nobody looks at is wallpaper.

cards.back: Zabbix: all-in-one, templates, traditional fleets. Prometheus: pull model, PromQL, cloud-native.
Metrics: numbers over time. Logs: events. Traces: request flows.
Utilization, Saturation, Errors / Rate, Errors, Duration.
Alert at 90%, clear at 80% - prevents flapping.
Threshold, duration, severity, owner, runbook link.
Expired certs are a top-5 'embarrassing outage' cause.

cards.front: Synthetic transactions catch what pings miss
cards.back: Real user flows - login, checkout, query.
Weekly review: tune, delete, or route - >5 pages/week/person is broken.

quiz.q: Traditional Windows fleet, need monitoring fast. Choose?
quiz.explain: Templates per role = fast coverage.

quiz.q: Alert fires on one CPU spike then clears, repeatedly. Fix?
quiz.explain: Sustained + hysteresis kills flapping.

quiz.q: Server 'up' by ping but users can't log in. Missing?
choices: Synthetic transaction (log in like a user)
quiz.explain: Port-up != working; test the real flow.

quiz.q: On-call gets 20 pages/week, ignores them. You:
choices: Weekly alert review: tune thresholds, fix root causes, delete noise
quiz.explain: Fatigue is a tuning failure, not a staffing one.

quiz.q: New service launches. Monitoring plan?
choices: Golden signals + runbook-linked alerts + dashboard, baseline 2 weeks
quiz.explain: Instrument from day one.

quiz.q: DHCP scope hits 95% Monday. Should have:
quiz.explain: Capacity alerts precede outages.

quiz.q: Prometheus pull model means:
quiz.explain: Scrape-based collection.

quiz.q: Dashboard nobody looks at is:
choices: Wallpaper - design for an audience and a decision
quiz.explain: Dashboards serve decisions, not decoration.
